source_text: Yeah, so Saba is probably one of the inspiring examples for the person I talked with b/c he is Oakland based.  Broadly what's key here is the "demand side".  So, of course, if what people want is liquor, beer, wine, video games and casinos, tobacco, etc., then, within reasonable limits of regulation, that's what they are going to get.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) Agreed. A shop stocks what sells, so the owner's margin follows what residents actually want, and regulation only sets the outer limits. I've added your point to §3.8 (`12e7ba2`).

🈖 ("what's key here is the "demand side"") This is the earlier human-versus-tooling test at neighbourhood scale. Tooling changes how an intent gets carried out; it can't supply one. A co-op doesn't change that either. What it changes is *whose* preferences govern. In a residents' co-op it's the residents' wants that count, not an outsider's idea of what they ought to want. That's both why it's legitimate and why it might simply sell beer. So "is it in demand?" can only be answered in the inner loop, by asking residents and reading sales records, before anything is built.

㊟ (Saba) The Oakland link makes sense. Saba also sits on the side that doesn't require changing anyone's wants. It lowers the cost of stocking fresh food for owners who'd like to, and it leaves the deciding to customers. If your contact is building on that, the useful outer-loop question is what it would take to run a Saba in another city without Saba's staff. The answer is roughly the shared ordering, refrigeration logistics and sales records from §3.8.

🈸 (one decision) The co-op cases agent is still running. When it reports, shall I add a Saba-style outer-loop sketch to the mission, as something concrete you could show your contact? Or would you rather keep the mission at the survey level for now?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) This is a good test case, and there's real evidence on both sides of your "(and possibly not)". I've written it up as a worked scattering in §3.8 (`e3305d5`). The short version: supply is a tooling problem a co-op can fix, while most of the gap is demand, which is a human problem.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
("and possibly not") The evidence against:
- **Allcott, Diamond & Dubé** (NBER, later published in *QJE*) used supermarket openings and families moving between neighbourhoods. They found no meaningful effect on healthy eating. Giving low-income households the same availability and prices as high-income ones closes only **9%** of the nutrition gap; the other 91% is demand. In R-node terms the gap sits mostly in C: habits, and knowing what a tomato is.
- **Renaissance Community Co-op** in Greensboro was a community-owned grocery in a food desert. It opened in 2016 after 18 years without a store, with $1.2M raised from members plus city and county grants. It closed in 2019 because sales were too low. The post-mortem's summary: "people had developed other habits."

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (but at store level) Healthy-corner-store programmes do report that when shops stock fresh produce, customers buy more of it and fewer sugary drinks. Both findings can be true: a real effect store by store can still close little of the gap across a population.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
(two co-ops in one phrase) "Corner store co-op" can mean two different things:
- **A consumer co-op store** (the Renaissance model). It replaces the corner shop, so it carries every cost: capital, lease, staff, demand.
- **A purchasing co-op of existing corner stores.** It keeps the shops and their owners, the component that has lasted (NYC has 14,000+ bodegas, about 12 for every grocery store). It pools only the hard part. Distributors' minimum orders are too big for a small store, and fresh food needs refrigeration. **Saba Grocers** in Oakland does exactly this: refrigeration plus collective purchasing so shops can order below wholesale minimums. It has grown from 3 pilot stores in 2020 to 14 by July 2025.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
(where the outer loop fits) The tech side is small and cheap:
- pooled ordering across stores
- item-level sales and spoilage records
- checks against SNAP/WIC stocking rules
